analysis.one_liner: Counts military and veteran education benefits as federal money in the 90/10 rule for-profit colleges must meet.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to close the GI Bill loophole in the 90/10 rule died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 90/10 rule, a for-profit college must draw at least 10% of its revenue from non-federal sources. Today, Pentagon tuition-assistance dollars and most GI Bill payments do not count as federal money, so colleges can count them toward that 10% — meaning schools can legally be funded entirely by federal and military money. This bill would count military and veteran education benefits as federal money, impose escalating penalties for schools that fail the rule (from blocking new-enrollment funds to a two-year ban), publicize violators on federal websites, and apply the rule for two years after a for-profit school converts to nonprofit status.
analysis.who_benefits: Servicemembers and veterans using DoD tuition assistance or the GI Bill, who would be steered away from schools that live entirely off those benefits, and taxpayers, who would stop funding colleges that have no skin in the game from non-federal revenue. Veterans would also see a 'caution flag' on the GI Bill Comparison Tool for schools out of compliance.

how_it_helps.text: Counts education benefits under chapters 30, 31, 33, and 35 of title 38 and DoD programs as federal educational assistance, closing the loophole that let for-profit colleges count GI Bill and Pentagon tuition dollars toward the 10% non-federal revenue requirement.

Sets tiered penalties for schools failing the rule: no federal or military education funds for new enrollments after one failure, continued cutoffs after a second consecutive failure, and ineligibility for all federal educational assistance for at least two years after a third consecutive failure.

Requires public disclosure on the Department of Education's College Navigator and the VA's GI Bill Comparison Tool of any for-profit school out of compliance, including a caution flag and the applicable sanction.
Applies the 90/10 rule to a for-profit institution for two years after it converts to nonprofit status, closing a conversion path schools used to escape scrutiny.
Requires annual reports to Congress breaking down, from audited financial statements, how much of each for-profit school's revenue comes from federal educational assistance.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges, which would lose eligibility for GI Bill and Pentagon tuition dollars if federal money plus military benefits exceed 90% of their revenue. Some veterans enrolled at schools that fail the rule could see those schools cut off from new federal funding, restricting where they can use benefits.

drawbacks.text: The penalty structure and appeals process have real carve-outs: a school can appeal up to three consecutive times (five in ten years) and keep receiving funds during the appeal by showing clean records and 'high-quality' programs, and the bill excludes Post-9/11 GI Bill housing and book stipends from the federal count, leaving some veteran dollars outside the rule.
The new rules would not take effect until the 2022 institutional fiscal year, giving affected schools years of lead time to adjust or plan conversions before any penalty applies.
Veterans who prefer education options at for-profit schools would have fewer places to use their benefits if schools lose eligibility, a cost borne by students rather than the schools' owners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward: schools that currently collect nearly all their revenue from federal and military programs would have to find real non-federal funding or lose access to new veteran and Pentagon enrollments. The main cost falls on the schools themselves, not on veterans directly, though veterans attending flagged schools could lose access to those programs. The bill is not aggressive — it keeps an appeals escape hatch, excludes housing and book stipends, and delays effective dates to 2022 — so it softens its own enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2019 and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it never reached the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Carper introduced the bill on November 14, 2019, joined by original cosponsors Senator Lankford, Senator Cassidy, and Senator Tester, and it was read twice and referred to the HELP Committee.
The bill drew five cosponsors in total, three Republicans and two Democrats.
The Senate took no further action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in its action history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that rely on GI Bill and Pentagon tuition dollars are better off; the loophole letting them count military benefits as non-federal revenue remained open through the end of the Congress. Veterans and taxpayers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had five Senate cosponsors split three Republicans and two Democrats, so its death was not a partisan vote but a committee that never acted.

industries.note: The bill would make GI Bill and Pentagon tuition dollars count as federal revenue, so schools that currently live almost entirely off federal and military money would lose eligibility for new veteran enrollments unless they changed how they fund themselves. It also targets the nonprofit-conversion path some for-profit chains used to escape oversight, and would put caution flags on violators in the VA's comparison tool veterans use to pick schools.

industries.industry: Veterans Education Success and veteran service organizations advocating 90/10 reform
industries.note: Reform groups had pushed for years to close this loophole; this bill would have advanced their goal, though its appeal process and stipend exclusions fall short of the full fix they sought. This is a policy-aligned interest rather than an industry, included because it shaped the debate around 90/10 reform.
